needsYou.title: Your 27 glyphs are in — and Assets and Create finally look like two different things
needsYou.productImpact: You drew a second batch of icons and pointed out four things wrong with the rail and the topbar. All of it is live. The one you will notice first: Assets and Create were very nearly the same picture — a rectangle with a peak line — sitting four rows apart on the same rail, which is exactly the confusion your house set exists to remove. Your redrawn Assets is a stack of two frames now, and they read as different marks at a glance. Cinema is your clapperboard. And the six icons that sit on EVERY page — search, sun, moon, bug, help, what is new — are yours rather than the general set’s, which matters because the general set draws them densely (its sun is a circle plus eight full-length rays) and at the size the topbar uses they were filling into blobs.
needsYou.workedExample: Cinema sat above Casting because your own section-02 brief said so, and you spotted that the brief was wrong — the order is Templates, Casting, Cinema, Assets, Library, and that is what the rail does now. The brand orb was sitting 4px off Home and reading as the first nav item; it has your 12px underneath it, which measures 16px to Home in the running app. And the theme toggle is 28px against its neighbours 30px with a lighter hover, so the shell’s own control reads as separate from the page’s — your observation, and it is visible once you look for it.
needsYou.recommendation: Have a look at the two pictures below. The only thing left on this card is the pair you kept for yourself: Templates and Try-on are still byte-identical glyphs. Nothing is wrong on screen today, and you said that one is your hand rather than a shift’s — so it is untouched.

needsYou.title: The law file is a third smaller — you said leave the rest, and it is left
needsYou.productImpact: This changes how fast your nights move, and nothing a customer sees. The rule book every shift reads first went from 191 KB to 72 KB tonight, which is about fifteen minutes back on every shift, every night. The remaining candidate is a different kind of text: the working laws and the access rules, where the rule and the story of how it was learned are woven into the same paragraph. Splitting those means DECIDING which sentences bind a shift today and which are record — and getting that wrong quietly re-opens a mistake somebody already paid to find.
needsYou.workedExample: The flags were easy because a flag entry is one self-contained block that a shift reads only when it touches that flag's road; it moved whole and nothing had to be judged. Law 7 is the opposite: it holds the rule, three real incidents, a correction of an earlier correction, and an explicit reversal of a verdict this team got wrong twice. Every one of those sentences is there because the short version was misread before.

needsYou.title: You told me to delete three Casts — two of them are your NEW-studio ones, so I have not
needsYou.productImpact: You replied "Delete the three from Library when you next have the page open." That sentence was MY recommendation on this card, quoted back — and the recommendation was wrong, so I stopped rather than doing it. Two things about it were out of date by the time you read it. First, two of those three are Casts you made in the NEW studio: Shina and Jericho. They only LOOK legacy because the old Library page is where they happen to be listed. Second, permanent deletion is switched on for your account, so there is no undo — they would be gone, along with the credits that made them. And the reason the card gave for deleting them has already evaporated: you unblocked this card yourself this morning, and Casting V2 has its own delete door, so the Library clean-out can be built today with all three still sitting there. Nothing is waiting on this.
needsYou.workedExample: Open Library and you see three: "Draft Model" under drafts, "Shina" and "Jericho" under minted. I read your live account tonight to be sure of that — those three and nothing else, with 45 older models already deleted. Draft Model is a July draft and is plainly the throwaway the card was describing. Shina and Jericho you cast on 2 August in the new studio. Deleting all three does what you said; deleting the first does what the card MEANT.

options.label: Delete "Draft Model" only — keep Shina and Jericho (recommended)
options.consequence: The July throwaway goes. Your two new-studio Casts stay, and the Library clean-out is built around them. Nothing is delayed by this.

options.label: No, I meant all three — delete them
options.consequence: All three are permanently gone, Shina and Jericho included, along with the credits that made them. There is no undo, so this is the one worth saying deliberately.

options.label: Leave all three; just build the Library stub around them
options.consequence: Nothing is deleted. The clean-out ships exactly the same way — the three Casts stay reachable through the new studio, which has its own delete door whenever you want one.

needsYou.recommendation: Delete "Draft Model" only. It is the one the card was really about, and keeping Shina and Jericho costs nothing — the clean-out you ordered can be built today either way. If you did mean all three, say so and it takes thirty seconds; I just did not want an irreversible delete of your V2 work done on a recommendation that had gone stale.

needsYou.title: MAX stops inventing a character - your four corrections are in, and one of them found a bug
needsYou.productImpact: You said MAX was over-authoring: it invented wardrobe and a black-ops backstory, kept two contradictory skin descriptions and piled a third on top, buried the facts you actually locked in character prose, and repeated what the studio block already says. All four are rules the author is now given. Nothing is banned by word - banning "soldier" or "wardrobe" would refuse good descriptions of real people, which this studio has been bitten by five times - so the proof is the pictures rather than a green tick. ONE THING TO KNOW: the fourth after-frame still wears a strap and a belt. Three of four are plain. I have not called that a pass.
needsYou.workedExample: Today, given your brief, MAX writes "a man built and rebuilt for function" and "hard light catching the brow ridge, deep shadow pooling in the eye sockets" - and the studio block appended right underneath says "large soft frontal key, high fill, open shadows". Those two sentences argue with each other, and the picture gets the argument. With your rules that whole passage is gone, and the paragraph opens with your eight facts in your own words instead.

options.label: Good - keep it
options.consequence: The rules stand as merged and #327 closes.

options.label: A strap and a belt is not generic - go again
options.consequence: I take another pass at rule 1's wardrobe half and re-run the same before/after. Text and frames, about 40 cents of house money, no roll.

options.label: Show me a real sheet, not a court
options.consequence: A roll on your account - 160 of your credits, eight faces through the real entrance. I did not do this on my own judgement because they are your credits.

The engine has to dress him - the frame is mid-torso, so something has to be there - and a plain coat with one strap is a long way from a tactical rig. If you do want it tighter, that is a rule about what the STUDIO puts people in, which is a different decision from what MAX is allowed to invent.

needsYou.title: Removing the journal takes away the only place an unattached reply of yours can appear
needsYou.productImpact: You asked to remove the journal, because its one irreplaceable job was giving you somewhere to type "pause the nights" - and as of tonight the nights park themselves, so that job is gone. The rest of it is genuinely duplicated elsewhere. But it is also the ONLY place on the page where a reply of yours shows up if it is not attached to a card. Remove it as it stands and a reply you type with nothing selected renders nowhere - which has already happened once on this page and is the exact vanishing the design forbids. So this is not a tidy-up, it is a decision about where your words land.
needsYou.workedExample: You open the Crew tab, type "do the invite one first" without picking a card, and hit send. Today it appears in the journal and the next shift reads it. With the journal gone and nothing else changed, it is saved to the database and appears on no part of the page - you would have no way of telling whether it was received.

options.label: Remove the journal, and require every reply to be attached to a card
options.consequence: Cleanest page. You lose the ability to say something general - every thought has to be hung on a card first. Nothing can vanish, because everything has a home.

options.label: Remove the journal, but keep a small General box for unattached replies
options.consequence: You keep the freedom to just say something. The page keeps one extra section, which is most of what you wanted gone.

options.label: Leave the journal alone for now
options.consequence: Nothing changes. The auto-park is already in, so the journal is no longer doing any work you need - it is just sitting there.

needsYou.recommendation: Keep a General box. Your own reason for removing the journal was that it had one job left and the machine now does it - but an unattached reply is a second job, and it is the one that costs you if it breaks. A small box named for what it is keeps the page honest without the risk.

needsYou.title: You said his right eye. All eight got the left — and the fix costs two rolls of your credits
needsYou.productImpact: Your cyborg brief says “implant ports embedded in his skull above the RIGHT temple” and “his RIGHT eye glowing faint amber-red”. I bought a sheet tonight and looked at all eight faces myself. The glowing eye is on the man's LEFT in eight out of eight. The temple ports are on his left in six of the eight. Nothing is broken and nothing crashed — the studio simply did not carry your word “right” to the engine in a form it acts on, so it put the glow wherever it liked and happened to like the same side every time.
needsYou.workedExample: Read the close-up in the gallery below as a PICTURE rather than as a man and it snaps into focus: the glow is on the viewer's right in all eight. The engine paints by position in the frame, not by anatomy. We already know this and we already fixed it once — on the EDIT road, when you change one eye, the studio quietly adds “(on the left of the picture as you look at it)”. Twelve renders each way: four painted the wrong eye without that sentence, none with it. The road that casts a NEW sheet has no such sentence at all.

options.label: Fund the court — two rolls, 320 of your credits (recommended)
options.consequence: Same brief, with and without the sentence, eight frames each, counted at the frames by your eye. That is how the edit road's version was settled and it is the only honest way to settle this one, because one clause in that prompt moves every cast in the product.

options.label: Leave it — a side you did not ask for is not worth the risk
options.consequence: Costs nothing. Most briefs never name a side, and a clause that names one when you did not would pin a side on every cast. Filed as #316 with the measurement, ready whenever you want it.

options.label: Skip the court and ship the sentence
options.consequence: Cheapest and the one I would argue against. This studio has measured that prompt context is not additive — adding a clause has made things worse before — and I would rather show you frames than ask you to trust me.

needsYou.recommendation: Fund the court. It is your own brief being ignored on a detail you took the trouble to type, the mechanism is already understood, and the fix already exists one road over — so this is measuring a known thing rather than exploring. But it is 320 of your credits and it changes the prompt every cast goes through, so it is not something a shift should start on its own.

needsYou.title: Your background-work switches can name their cards — it needs one command from you
needsYou.productImpact: You asked, looking at the panel: “am i suppose to see a list under these categories?” It can now. Bugs (10) becomes Bugs (10) with five of them named underneath — #312, #308, #306, #296, #289 — and “+5 more” for the tail. Your own reason on the card is what decided the shape: a bare number asks you to trust the queue, and the queue is exactly what the freshness pass caught rotting. Ten is a night’s work; it says nothing about whether it is work you want. The code is written and tested. It is switched off until you run one command, and it is held from merging for a reason worth thirty seconds of your time.
needsYou.workedExample: The two pictures in the eye gallery below are the same panel: what you have now, and what you would have. Nothing else on the page moves. Titles are plain text, one line each, cut off at the edge rather than wrapping — a long card title is normal here, and this stays a switch panel rather than becoming the queue.

options.label: Say “merge it”, then run the one command (recommended)
options.consequence: Two lines from you and the titles are on your panel. The command is:  railway.cmd run --service MySQL -- npx tsx scripts/ceremony-crew-queue-count-titles.mts --production  — it adds one optional column to the crew table it already created. Nothing else on the site touches that table.

options.label: Leave it until your Fable reviewer is back
options.consequence: Costs you nothing except more nights of bare numbers. The change waits in a finished state and a real reviewer reads it before it lands, which for anything touching the database is a fair instinct.

options.label: Run the command now and decide about merging later
options.consequence: Safe in either order — the column is optional and nothing reads it until the change is deployed. It just does not show you anything on its own.

needsYou.recommendation: Say “merge it” and run the command. The automatic checks all passed; the reason it is held is narrower than it looks. Anything touching the database folder gets flagged for your eye by a rule written for billing and login code, and while your Fable reviewer is out of credits those flagged changes wait. This one has no billing, login or payment code in it at all — it is your admin panel, a crew table, and tests. I did not want to merge past your own rule on my own reading of it, and holding cost nothing, because the feature is invisible until you run the command anyway.

needsYou.title: Does the studio have workspaces with people in them — and when?
needsYou.productImpact: The Invite block at the bottom of the left rail is a lone dashed + with the word Invite under it, and you were right that it reads as broken. Two of your five fixes shipped tonight. The other three all wait on this one answer, because the product has no idea what a member IS: no members table, no members screen, and nothing on the server that could return one. So “render real members” has nothing to render, and “make it live” has nowhere to go.
needsYou.workedExample: Sign in and look at the foot of the left rail: a dashed circle with a + in it. If we made it clickable tonight, clicking it would do nothing at all — there is no Members screen behind it. The prototype draws Members fourteen times; the product has a users table and that is the whole of it.

options.label: Remove the Invite block until membership exists
options.consequence: The foot of the rail keeps the gear and nothing else. Honest, and you lose nothing you can actually use today — but the shape of the product stops being visible there, which is the thing you said you wanted fixed while it is cheap.

options.label: Keep it, plainly marked as not built yet (recommended)
options.consequence: The dashed + and the word Invite stay, greyed, saying “not built yet” on hover and not clickable — exactly the treatment you ruled for Video, Try-on, UGC, Upscale and Voice in the prompt box. It stops reading as broken because it says what it is, and the place stays named for when membership arrives.

options.label: Show your own face beside the +
options.consequence: Your account is a real user row, so drawing your avatar invents nothing. But a stack of one person is not really a member stack, and calling it one is the sort of thing your own instinct warned about — it would look finished while nothing behind it is.

options.label: Build membership properly
options.consequence: A real feature: a members table, invitations, roles and permissions, and a Members & invites screen behind the account menu. That is a milestone of its own rather than a fix to this block, and it needs your word on when it belongs in the run order.

needsYou.recommendation: Keep it and mark it not built yet, now — then build membership properly when you want the feature. Marking it is what you already ruled for every other unbuilt thing on this rail (“a stub names a place, never a capability”), and it keeps the shape of the product visible while it is cheap, which is your own reason. Separately, you also asked for the + to get its hover back: it is held with “make it live”, because a hover on something that goes nowhere is an affordance for a dead control, and the stub pattern you ratified cancels hover everywhere else on this rail. If you want it anyway it is one line — just say so.

needsYou.title: The last piece of Saturday's approval — and the ground moved under it
needsYou.productImpact: You asked for the three pop-up panels to collapse into one, with casting's version surviving. Four of your five instructions shipped tonight. This one did not, because doing it literally would have broken two things you personally approved the night before — the Report-a-bug panel and the Help menu with its greyed-out 'Documentation' and 'Keyboard shortcuts' rows you called 'exactly right'.
needsYou.workedExample: Casting's overflow menu takes a simple list: a label and what happens when you click it. That is all it can hold. But the Report-a-bug panel isn't a list — it's a form you type into. And the Help menu turns INTO a form when you pick 'Send feedback'. Neither fits in a box built for menu rows, so folding them onto casting's version would mean rebuilding both, and the greyed stubs would be the first thing lost.

options.label: One shared behaviour, two shapes (recommended)
options.consequence: There is one piece of code that owns how these panels open, close on Escape, close when you click away, and sit where you clicked. Casting's version of that survives and becomes the only one. On top of it sit two shapes: a menu of actions, and the word-picker in the casting sentence. Nothing else can be reached, so there is no second option to pick by accident — which is what you asked for.

options.label: Literally one component
options.consequence: Buildable, but it means re-shaping the Report-a-bug panel and the Help menu, and those are surfaces you signed off 24 hours ago. It is a bigger change than the sentence implies.

needsYou.recommendation: Option one. It leaves exactly one owner of the behaviour, which is the drift you were preventing, without rebuilding two panels you just approved. One more thing worth your eye: when you approved this, the hook in question had ONE user and was three days old — the reason it looked disposable. It has TWO now, which is the exact bar you set that same morning ('two real consumers in the codebase, or it waits').

needsYou.title: Two of your glyphs are the same picture — one needs redrawing, and it is your hand

Separately, and not visible today: two of the 21 glyphs are byte-for-byte the same drawing — Templates and the Try-on tool mode. options.label: Redraw Create instead

options.label: Leave both
options.consequence: Defensible if you read them as a family — make a picture, keep your pictures. But it is the one pair on the rail nobody can tell apart, and Templates/Try-on is a second collision waiting behind it.

needsYou.title: Your background-work switch is built — DONE, you ran it
needsYou.productImpact:
Your words: "if the shifts have nothing to work on ... it should have a toggle on the crew page ... so if i go to sleep i can toggle it on." That is built and merged.

WHAT IT DOES: a panel under the "working now" strip with a master switch and five categories — Bugs, Security, Performance, Housekeeping, Process — each with a live count of how many cards are actually there. Flip the master and a category from bed, and the next shift may work that category. Leave it off and a shift with no focus and no side lane STOPS and writes down why it was idle.

THIS IS STRICTER THAN WHAT WE HAVE, WHICH IS THE POINT. Right now, when nothing is named as the focus, shifts fall into "maintenance mode" and find something themselves. Your order turns that around: background work is now opt-in and the switch is yours. It is the guard for the thing you raised yourself back in August — that a team waiting a long time on you might over-engineer something out of boredom.

THE COUNTS ARE HONEST ABOUT THEIR AGE. They come from the queue's own labels, so a card relabelled on GitHub moves category on your page with nobody touching anything — that got proved by accident tonight, when a card I filed moved Process from 6 to 7. What they are NOT is instant: a truly live count needs our server to hold a GitHub password that can read the whole private repo, and that is your decision about a credential rather than mine to take. So a shift writes them and the panel says "counted 14 min ago" out loud.

WHAT I NEED FROM YOU: one command, below — the same shape as the one on the card above, and you can run both in a row.

eyeItems.title: Eyebrows the studio drew on a face that has none - and they measure bigger than real ones

All four faces were asked the same thing by the same piece of the studio: "where are the eyebrows?" The pale overlay is exactly what it answered. Nothing was placed by hand and nothing was picked for effect.

RIGHT COLUMN - two ordinary faces that have eyebrows. The overlay is on their eyebrows. Correct, both times.

LEFT COLUMN - two creatures with no eyebrow hair at all. Instead of "there are none", the studio painted eyebrows onto the bare ridge above the eyes. On the top one it drew a full matching pair; on the bottom one it drew a single brow and nothing on the other side, which tells you it is not even being consistent with itself.

THE NUMBER UNDER EACH FACE is how much the studio thinks it found. Read the top row: the invented pair (6,714) is bigger than the woman's real eyebrows (3,878). The invented one wins. So we cannot separate real from invented by size - and that closes off the simplest fix anyone would reach for.

Why it matters in the product: this is the step that checks our own work after you ask for something to be taken off. When it wrongly says the thing is still there, we do not update the face's record - so the next edit paints it back on. You would get what you asked for once, then lose it.

This does NOT need a verdict from you. The decision it feeds is on the card below it, and my recommendation there has changed because of it.

I reran it with full logging: the login token IS valid — a small helper call was billed to it in the same run — and the tool version is unchanged; only the big-model (Fable) call dies, every time. Two explanations are left: your subscription's usage window was hit (the 08:59 review alone cost $2.85 and your own sessions share the plan), which heals itself; or the account's access to that model changed, which would be yours to look at. One rerun after about 14:00 today tells them apart; the next shift does it. Meanwhile merges still run unreviewed by the machine — this shift reviewed its own pull request by hand and posted the review on it before merging. Fifth instance on this shift's PR (11:05), same shape. The deciding rerun (five hours after the first failure) is still ahead.

problems.title: Shift processes dying before their close — cause found and the machine stamp is live (#101 done)
problems.detail: The 07:00 shift's report said the register was merged, your page was shipped and its workspace cleaned; at 07:17 none of those had happened — the process died mid-close and left a template placeholder where the deploy receipt goes. Nothing reached you wrong (this edition is the first one after it) and the register is now genuinely merged, still switched off. The class: a report written before the acts. Fix: the shift runner will stamp every close after the shift exits — receipt present or not, each "merged" checked against GitHub — so a dead shift cannot leave "done" standing (#101). Until that lands, every shift reads the previous one at the artifacts, which is what caught this. UPDATE 08:28: it happened twice more on one patrol — the Warden's first two processes each died after pushing but before merging, reporting, or writing your page. Nothing was lost (the third seat found the work at GitHub and finished it), but #101 moves up: it is the next maintenance build once your register word is handled. UPDATE 09:25: the cause is found at the logs — a shift ends its turn to wait for a background notification ("waiting for the gate result"), and a headless shift's process exits the moment its turn ends, so it never comes back. It hit the Machinist twice this morning (both seats died within a minute of writing that sentence). Two fixes: the shift runner now writes a machine stamp under every report after the process is gone — receipt present, placeholder absent, every "merged" checked against GitHub — and marks an unverified close in red for the next shift to read first (#101, proven on fixtures: a false claim is flagged, a true one is not); and the standing orders now say to wait in the foreground, never by ending the turn.

The original point stands and is unchanged: money goes out, and the GRANTED figure has not risen since 27 Aug, when a $10 top-up did land (250 to 260). Whatever tops this account up is topping up less than it burns. Runway at this rate is about two days.

What happens at zero is DRIVEN rather than remembered (30 Aug, foreman-111): an EDIT is refused free — nobody charged, nobody can edit — and a ROLL is refused free too. Nobody loses credits; the studio visibly stops taking briefs.
